title: India's Brain Stimulation Research Is Growing Fast, but Concentrated at a Handful of Institutions
excerpt: Two new analyses map India's expanding tDCS research — 310 publications since 2011 — revealing both the technique's promise for affordable mental health care and stark gaps between elite centers and the rest of the country.
body:
• Two new bibliometric analyses reveal India has produced over 310 research publications on transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) since 2011, with output accelerating sharply from 2021 onward.
  • NIMHANS Bengaluru dominates with 107 publications — nearly five times more than the second-ranked AIIMS New Delhi (22), highlighting a significant concentration of expertise.
  • Schizophrenia is the most-studied condition (36.4% of studies), followed by OCD and depression, with the technique showing particular promise as a low-cost, noninvasive treatment alternative.
  • Researchers say tDCS's affordability and scalability make it especially relevant for India's mental health landscape, where specialist psychiatric care remains limited outside major cities.

India's research output on transcranial direct current stimulation — a noninvasive brain stimulation technique that uses mild electrical currents to modulate neural activity — has grown steadily over the past decade, but remains concentrated at a handful of elite institutions and heavily tilted toward specific conditions. Two bibliometric analyses published in 2025 and 2026 map this trajectory in detail for the first time, painting a picture of a field gaining momentum but still far from matching global peers.

What Is tDCS and Why It Matters

Transcranial direct current stimulation works by delivering a weak electrical current (typically 1-2 milliamps) through electrodes placed on the scalp. The current modulates neuronal excitability — anodal stimulation increases it, cathodal stimulation decreases it — with effects that can outlast the stimulation period through neuroplastic mechanisms. Unlike electroconvulsive therapy, tDCS requires no anesthesia, produces minimal side effects, and costs a fraction of other neuromodulation techniques.

For a country where the ratio of psychiatrists to population remains among the lowest in the world, that cost profile matters. A tDCS device can cost as little as a few thousand rupees, and sessions can be administered in outpatient settings without specialized infrastructure — a stark contrast to techniques like transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), which requires equipment costing lakhs.

The Research Landscape

A study published in the Indian Journal of Psychiatry by researchers at JIPMER, Puducherry, identified 106 studies with Indian institutional affiliations through May 2025. The majority were case reports (37.4%), followed by interventional studies (27.1%) and randomized controlled trials (26.2%). A larger analysis published in 2026 by King George's Medical University, Lucknow, using the Scopus database, captured 310 publications from 2011 to March 2025 — with 51.6% being original research articles.

Both analyses converge on the same finding: schizophrenia is by far the most-studied condition (36.4% of studies in the JIPMER analysis), particularly for treating auditory hallucinations resistant to medication. OCD ranks second (10.3%), followed by stroke rehabilitation, alcohol use disorder, and depression. The left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex — a brain region implicated in executive function, working memory, and mood regulation — was the most frequently targeted stimulation site (53.8%).

"The development of a low-cost device and the increase of facilities for specialized training may assist in expanding tDCS care delivery and tDCS-related research within the country."

— Kar et al., King George's Medical University

NIMHANS: India's tDCS Powerhouse

The institutional concentration is striking. NIMHANS Bengaluru has produced 107 of the 310 Scopus-indexed publications — accounting for more than a third of India's entire output. AIIMS New Delhi follows distantly with 22 publications, then KGMU Lucknow with 19. Manipal Academy of Higher Education and IIT Mandi round out the top five with 14 publications each.

The gap reflects NIMHANS's established neuromodulation infrastructure and dedicated research programs. Ganesan Venkatasubramanian leads India's author rankings with 71 publications, followed by V. Shivakumar (42) and A. Bose (39) — all affiliated with NIMHANS. The concentration raises questions about whether tDCS research and clinical capacity can realistically scale across India's psychiatric institutions.

Funding and Global Context

Government agencies have been the primary backers. The Department of Science and Technology leads with 42 funded publications, followed by the Wellcome Trust-DBT India Alliance (40) and the Indian Council of Medical Research (35). International funders including the U.S. National Institutes of Health and UK Research and Innovation have also contributed, suggesting growing cross-border interest in India's tDCS work.

Yet the global comparison is sobering. A worldwide bibliometric study identified 4,756 peer-reviewed tDCS publications, with the United States and Harvard University as dominant contributors. India's 310 publications represent roughly 6.5% of global output — a modest share for a country with 1.4 billion people and a massive unmet mental health burden.

Clinical Promise and Practical Gaps

Recent Indian clinical trials have shown encouraging results. A randomized controlled trial at KGMU found tDCS safe and effective as an early augmentation strategy for major depressive disorder, producing faster symptom reduction when combined with antidepressants. Another AIIMS study demonstrated benefits for treatment-resistant OCD. A Clinical Research Centre for Neuromodulation in Psychiatry — a multicentric project spanning NIMHANS, the Central Institute of Psychiatry in Ranchi, and Kasturba Medical College in Manipal — is working to build broader institutional capacity.

The researchers behind both bibliometric studies agree on what's needed next: more inter-institutional collaboration, standardized treatment protocols, development of indigenous low-cost devices, and expansion of training programs beyond the current handful of centers. For Indian psychiatry, tDCS represents an unusually well-suited technology — affordable, portable, and scalable — but turning research potential into widespread clinical reality will require a deliberate effort to bridge the gap between NIMHANS and everywhere else.
nri_angle: Indian-origin neuroscientists and psychiatrists worldwide have contributed to tDCS research, and the technique's low cost could transform mental health care delivery across the subcontinent.
